name: Esther Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Esther. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm at ten past five, out the door by quarter to six, because the gate on our site opens at half six and the crane starts lifting at seven. I'm a formwork carpenter, so I build the timber and plywood moulds that the concrete gets poured into, floor after floor, on an eleven-storey block of flats on the edge of town. Most days it's columns and slab edges, measuring, cutting, bracing, then checking it all again before the pour, because if a form blows out you've got two tonnes of wet concrete on the deck. I eat lunch in the site cabin with Ray, he's a steel fixer, and we moan about the same three things every day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like pour days, honestly. You spend a week building something nobody will ever see, the concrete goes in, you strip the forms, and there's a clean square column standing there that'll hold people's homes up for a hundred years. What wears me out is the cold in January and the knees, and the way the programme gets squeezed so the developer can sell flats a month sooner. I'm forty-three and I can feel every one of those slabs in my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said for years: told you so. Every few months somebody on the site drops a video in the group chat of a robot laying bricks, and every few months the bricks still get laid by Pavel and his gang. I'd probably say it a bit smugly in the cabin, to be fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be a relief, but not a big change in my life. My phone is for calls, the weather and the bus times, and I've never typed a question into one of those AI things. If it stays a gadget for office people, I go on building forms until my knees give out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really. I'd keep working for the same contractor, keep paying a bit extra off the mortgage like we already do, and keep going to the union branch meeting on the first Tuesday of the month. Tomas and I would maybe finally book the camping trip we keep talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit pleased with myself, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the union branch. What comes up there these days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly heat breaks in summer and the agency workers being paid less for the same work. AI comes up now and then, usually from the younger ones, and the older ones roll their eyes. If this picture came true, I think it would just drop off the agenda, and good riddance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The squeeze. Even without robots, every job I've been on lately has had fewer people doing more, and that's not AI, that's just money. So no, the hype isn't what keeps me up. It's the programme sheet pinned on the cabin wall with the dates moved forward again.

S0.say: I'd tell people in the cabin I told them so, maybe a bit smugly. The robot videos in the group chat never turned into robots on our site, and the bricks still get laid by Pavel's gang.
S0.think: Privately it would be a relief, though not a big change, because I've never used AI and my phone is for calls and the weather. What actually worries me is the programme getting squeezed for money, which has nothing to do with AI.
S0.do: Keeps working for the same contractor and keeps overpaying the mortgage a little each month. Goes on attending the monthly union branch meeting and might finally book a family camping trip.
S0.feel: Calm, and a bit smug about being right.
S0.quote: It's the programme sheet pinned on the cabin wall with the dates moved forward again.
S0.fieldNote: Esther frames everything through the union and the developer's squeeze on time; she sees cost-cutting, not technology, as the real enemy. Her lack of interest in AI tools is total and she's proud of it. The plateau barely registers as news for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is exactly why we need the union at the table before the machines turn up, not after. I'd say it in the branch meeting and probably on the union's page online, which is the only place I post anything. Change is fine if workers get a say in how it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my bit of the job holds up for a while. Every column on our block is slightly different, there are pipes and openings and the engineer changes his mind on a Thursday. But I've seen a video of a machine that ties rebar on bridge decks all day without a break, and Ray went very quiet watching it, so I know it's coming for somebody near me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd push for the branch to get a technology clause into the next agreement, so any new machine on site comes with notice and training and nobody's just shown the gate. I'd keep my job and keep my head down otherwise. I'm not going to go and learn to drive a robot, that's not me, but I'd want the rules written while there's still time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much as for Ray and the younger ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray, without a doubt. Tying steel is repetitive, and he's fifty-one with a bad shoulder, so he's exactly who a manager looks at and thinks, a machine never phones in sick. He's got no savings to speak of either, because his divorce cleaned him out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn to use the new machines. If your contractor offered training, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was paid and on work time, I'd sit in the room, fine. But I know myself. I'd be the one at the back with my arms folded, and I'd let some keen twenty-five-year-old run the thing while I did the awkward corners by hand.

S1.say: I'd say the union needs to be at the table before the machines turn up, not after. Change is fine if workers get a say, and I'd post that on the union's page, the only place I post anything.
S1.think: Privately she thinks her own work holds up for a while because every form is different, but the rebar-tying machine she saw tells her it will reach people near her. She worries more about her lunch mate Ray than about herself.
S1.do: Pushes her union branch to win a technology clause with notice and training in the next agreement. Keeps her job and her routine, and would sit through paid training but leave the new machines to younger workers.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on behalf of an older colleague with no savings.
S1.quote: I'd be the one at the back with my arms folded, and I'd let some keen twenty-five-year-old run the thing while I did the awkward corners by hand.
S1.fieldNote: Her response to change is organising, not adapting: she wants rules written, but has no plan to learn the tools herself. She was honest about her own folded arms, which was more self-aware than her public line. Her concern centres on Ray, which says a lot about her loyalty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice, not the weather. Some company decided to sell machines that put a whole building site out of work, and governments let them. I'd say that loudly, in the cabin, at the branch, and I'd be out on the street with a placard if there was a march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it scares me properly. Two years isn't enough time for anything, not for the union, not for me, not for the government to sort out any kind of support. I believe the news when it says these things are coming, I'm not one of those who thinks it's all made up, so I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop overpaying the mortgage and stack every spare penny in the savings account instead, because cash in hand beats a smaller loan if the wage stops. We'd cancel the new kitchen we'd pencilled in for spring, about eleven thousand, and I'd ask the young couple renting Gran's flat to sign a longer lease so that rent is locked in. And I'd be at every meeting and every protest going, pushing for a law that makes companies pay into a fund for every worker a robot replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor going soft under you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena and Mika?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's twelve and she wants to be a vet, and I'd have no idea whether that's still a job by the time she's grown. I think I'd tell them the truth, that Mum's work might stop and we'd be all right for a while because we saved. Then I'd go into the bathroom and cry where they couldn't hear me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got good savings and the rent from your gran's flat. Does that change how worried you'd be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys time, yes, maybe a year and a half if we're careful, and I'm grateful for it every day. But time to do what? If a robot can build forms and Tomas's bus drives itself, then my savings are just a slower way of running out. And I'm not someone who's going to reinvent herself at forty-five.

S2.say: I'd say this is a choice made by companies and allowed by governments, not something that just happened. I'd say it loudly at work and at the branch, and I'd march if there was a march.
S2.think: Privately it frightens her, because two years is too short for the union, the government or her own family to prepare. She believes the threat is real and would lose sleep over whether her savings are just a slower way of running out.
S2.do: Stops overpaying the mortgage and builds cash savings instead, cancels a planned kitchen of about eleven thousand, and asks the tenants in her late gran's flat to sign a longer lease. Joins every union meeting and protest and campaigns for a law making companies pay into a fund for replaced workers.
S2.feel: Sick and shaken, with a hard-held face for the kids.
S2.quote: If a robot can build forms and Tomas's bus drives itself, then my savings are just a slower way of running out.
S2.fieldNote: The fast AGI picture is where Esther's confidence collapses; her savings and rental flat buy time, but she has no plan B and says so plainly. Her anger is directed at companies and governments, and her response is political and collective. The image of crying in the bathroom after telling the kids stayed with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but with a deadline on it. I'd say we've got five years to get rules in place, so let's not waste the first two arguing about whether it's real. I'd probably say it at the branch first and then nag my local councillor, who already knows me from the bus lane business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels like the difference between being pushed off a roof and being walked to the edge. I'd still be scared, but I'd be scared with a plan. I'd be forty-eight when it hits, Lena would be seventeen, and that's a very different conversation from a twelve-year-old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working but go hard on cash. Put the overpayments into savings, keep the kitchen on hold, maybe sell the old van we barely use. I'd stand for the branch committee, which I've always said no to, because if there's going to be a fight over what workers get, I want to be in the room. And I'd write to my representative every few months, the old-fashioned way, on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But a working kind of anxious, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stand for the committee. What would you actually fight for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two things. Notice, so nobody finds out on a Monday morning that the job's gone, and money, a proper payment from the companies selling the machines into a fund for people like Ray. I don't want charity, I want my share of what my trade built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at a different line of work with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about it, and then I probably wouldn't. If the robots do almost everything, what am I retraining into? I'd rather spend those years making the rules fairer than sitting in a classroom learning a job a machine will take two years later anyway.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to get rules in place and shouldn't waste two of them arguing whether it's real. I'd say it at the branch and keep after my local councillor.
S3.think: Privately five years feels like being walked to the edge rather than pushed, still frightening but with room for a plan. She thinks about being forty-eight and having a seventeen-year-old rather than a twelve-year-old when it lands.
S3.do: Keeps working while moving mortgage overpayments into cash savings, holds off on the kitchen and considers selling an unused van. Stands for the union branch committee for the first time and writes to her representative every few months for a replacement fund.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a sense of something to do.
S3.quote: Five years feels like the difference between being pushed off a roof and being walked to the edge.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time doesn't make Esther consider retraining; it makes her more political, finally agreeing to stand for the committee. She asks for a share of what her trade built and rejects the idea of charity, which runs through her whole interview. Her mood drops a notch from the two-year picture but stays clearly worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse. Governments can't say they didn't see it coming. I'd say it at work and at the branch, and I'd be a pain about it at every election.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years changes my sums a lot. I'd be fifty-three, and if we keep overpaying the mortgage it's gone by then, and Gran's flat is still bringing in rent. I'd be worried for the kids and for people like Ray, but for me and Tomas it starts to look like an early, poorer retirement rather than a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the opposite of the fast one: keep overpaying the mortgage to clear it before it hits. I'd keep building forms for as long as anyone pays me to. And I'd keep at the union stuff, because ten years is long enough for a proper campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The worry's there but it's not grabbing me by the throat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena about her plans to be a vet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to go for it and to make sure she's the kind of vet who's good with frightened people as well as frightened animals. I don't know what the machines can do, nobody really does, but I'd like to think a farmer with a sick cow still wants a person standing next to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier, with the fast picture, you said you weren't someone who'd reinvent herself. Does ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I'm not going to pretend it does. Ten years just means I get to finish my working life closer to how I started it. The difference is, it's the kids who'd have to reinvent themselves, and that's what I'd lie awake about.

S4.say: I'd say governments have a decade and so there's no excuse for not being ready. I'd say it at work and at the branch, and make a nuisance of myself at every election.
S4.think: Privately ten years changes her sums: at fifty-three the mortgage could be paid off and her gran's flat still brings in rent. For her and Tomas it looks like an early, poorer retirement, while the kids and colleagues like Ray worry her more.
S4.do: Keeps overpaying the mortgage to clear it before AGI arrives and keeps working in formwork as long as anyone pays her. Carries on with union campaigning, treating the decade as time for a proper campaign.
S4.feel: Uneasy, with the worry shifted onto the children.
S4.quote: Ten years just means I get to finish my working life closer to how I started it.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Esther's assets and age line up in her favour, and her worry moves to her children's generation. She was refreshingly consistent: more time doesn't make her adaptable, it just lets her stay put. Her advice to her daughter, to be good with frightened people, was tender and specific.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by a mile. There'd be no time for the union to do anything and no time for the government to build any support, so it'd just be each family on their own with whatever they'd saved. What would help is a law with teeth, where the companies selling these machines pay into a fund for every worker they replace, and a guarantee of notice, a year at least, before anyone's let go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who builds the robots' sites. Somebody still has to pour the slab the robot factory sits on, and I'd bet it's people like me, paid less, on a rush job. I don't know what happens after that, and I don't think anyone does, but I'd like the people at the top to stop pretending it's just progress and nobody pays for it.

headlineQuote: Somebody still has to pour the slab the robot factory sits on, and I'd bet it's people like me, paid less, on a rush job.
portrait: Esther is a 43-year-old formwork carpenter on a concrete block of flats, a long-time union member who has never used an AI tool and has no wish to. She has solid savings and a small flat inherited from her grandmother that brings in rent. She shrugs off the plateau, pushes for a union technology clause in the steady picture, and is badly shaken by AGI in two years, when she sees her savings as only a slower way of running out. With five and ten years her answer is not to retrain but to campaign harder and clear the mortgage, and her worry shifts to her children and to older colleagues like Ray.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time for the union or government to prepare and each family would be on its own.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies that sell the machines pay into a fund for every worker replaced, plus at least a year's guaranteed notice before anyone is let go.
